definition: A substantial written report of an individual research or design project, submitted for an undergraduate award and examined by academic staff.
wrongs: A one-page leaflet advertising a product.
A group chat log with no argument or evidence.
A weekly timesheet from an internship.
why: An undergraduate thesis is a substantial individual report that is submitted and examined for the award.
example: A student submits an 8,000-word report of their timetable study, which two examiners read before the oral.
scenario: The award requires one examined report of your own project, not a leaflet or a chat log. Which submission meets that requirement?
scenarioWhy: The thesis is the substantial individual report submitted for examination.

definition: A plan, written before the main study, that states the question, rationale, method, and practical limits of the thesis.
wrongs: The finished thesis, including final results.
A reference list with no plan.
The oral defence slides shown after submission.
why: A proposal is an advance plan of question, reason, method, and limits, written so the study can be approved.
example: Before data collection, the student submits a proposal naming the question, the survey method, and the ten-week limit.
scenario: You have not collected data yet, and the department wants the question, method, and time limit approved. Which document is that?
scenarioWhy: The research proposal is the advance plan of question, rationale, method, and limits.

definition: The ordered set of chapters and front and back matter that the department requires for the thesis.
wrongs: Any order of notes, because structure does not matter if the topic is interesting.
The folder layout on the student's laptop.
The timetable of the supervisor's office hours.
why: Thesis structure is the required order of parts so examiners can find the argument, method, and evidence.
example: The department requires a title page, abstract, introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, and references.
scenario: Examiners cannot find the method because chapters are in a random order. Which requirement have you missed?
scenarioWrongs: A rule that any order is acceptable
scenarioWhy: Thesis structure is the required order of chapters and other matter.

definition: A short standalone summary of the question, method, main findings, and conclusion, written so a reader can judge relevance quickly.
wrongs: The full literature chapter copied into the front of the thesis.
A list of acknowledgements and thanks.
An introduction that depends on later chapters to make sense.
why: An abstract stands alone and briefly covers question, method, findings, and conclusion.
example: The 250-word abstract states the call-rate question, the two-group method, the significant drop, and the conclusion.
scenario: A reader has two minutes and must judge whether your thesis is relevant without opening the chapters. Which part should they read?
scenarioWrongs: A paragraph that only makes sense after chapter four
scenarioWhy: The abstract is a short standalone summary of question, method, findings, and conclusion.

definition: A small set of terms placed with the abstract that describe the topic and help others find the thesis.
wrongs: The entire abstract repeated as single words with no selection.
The student's password.
References that were never cited.
why: Keywords are selected search terms that describe the thesis for catalogues and databases.
example: Under the abstract the student lists password guidance, help-desk calls, and undergraduate training.
scenario: The library catalogue needs a few terms so others can find a thesis on help-desk calls. Which item supplies them?
scenarioWhy: Keywords are the short topic terms used to find the thesis.

definition: The opening chapter that sets the context, problem, aim, and the outline of the rest of the thesis.
wrongs: The chapter that reports statistical tables with no context.
The reference list.
The appendix of raw transcripts.
why: The introduction orients the reader with context, problem, aim, and a map of the thesis.
example: Chapter 1 explains rising reset calls, states the aim, and outlines the later chapters.
scenario: Readers need the context, the problem, the aim, and a map of the chapters before the literature. Which chapter is that?
scenarioWhy: The introduction chapter sets context, problem, aim, and the outline of the thesis.

definition: A precise account of the issue the thesis addresses and why that issue matters.
wrongs: A topic label such as passwords, with no issue and no reason it matters.
The list of software used.
The student's biography.
why: A problem statement defines the issue and its importance, which a bare topic label does not.
example: The statement says first-year reset calls have doubled and staff cannot tell whether short videos would reduce them.
scenario: The draft says only passwords. Examiners ask what is wrong and why it matters. Which passage must you add?
scenarioWrongs: A longer topic label with no issue
scenarioWhy: A problem statement gives a precise issue and the reason it matters.

definition: The overall purpose of the thesis, plus the specific checkable outcomes that together achieve that purpose.
wrongs: A single vague hope to look at the area.
The hypothesis test result, which is a finding rather than an intention.
The word-count limit set by the department.
why: The aim is the overall purpose, and objectives are the specific outcomes used to achieve it.
example: The aim is to evaluate a short video; one objective is to compare reset calls between video and text groups.
scenario: You need an overall purpose and specific outcomes an examiner can check. Which pair should the introduction contain?
scenarioWrongs: Only the hope to look at the area
scenarioWhy: Aim and objectives state the purpose and the checkable outcomes of the thesis.

definition: The chapter that critically synthesises prior work and shows the gap the thesis will address.
wrongs: A dump of quotations in date order with no argument.
The chapter that presents the new study's own results.
The appendix of the survey form.
why: The literature review chapter builds an argument from prior work and justifies the gap.
example: The chapter compares studies of training videos, notes that call rates are rarely measured, and links that gap to the aim.
scenario: Prior studies are summarised one by one and never compared, so no gap appears. Which revision does the literature review chapter need?
scenarioAnswer: A critical synthesis that ends in the gap
scenarioWrongs: More quotations still in date order only
Moving the new results into that chapter
Replacing it with the blank survey form
scenarioWhy: The literature review chapter must synthesise prior work and show the gap.

definition: Combining sources so they build an argument, rather than summarising each source in isolation.
wrongs: Writing one paragraph per paper with no links between them.
Copying a single paper and changing a few words.
Deleting all sources to make the chapter original.
why: Synthesis connects sources to support a claim about what the literature, taken together, shows.
example: Three studies are discussed together to show that short guidance helps recall but has not been tested on call volume.
scenario: Each paragraph describes one paper and never links them. Which change produces synthesis?
scenarioAnswer: Group the papers around a claim they jointly support
scenarioWrongs: Keep one isolated paragraph per paper
Copy one paper and tweak the words
scenarioWhy: Synthesis combines sources into an argument instead of leaving them as separate summaries.

definition: An acknowledgement, in the required style, of the source of an idea, quotation, figure, or result used in the thesis.
wrongs: A thank-you in the acknowledgements that names no source for a claim.
A URL pasted with no author, date, or title when the style requires them.
A footnote that says source unknown on a borrowed paragraph.
why: A citation identifies the source of borrowed material in the form the required style demands.
example: A claim about call rates is followed by an author-year citation that matches the reference list.
scenario: You use another author's finding in the introduction. Which addition is a proper citation?
scenarioAnswer: An author-year pointer that matches a full reference
scenarioWrongs: A thank-you that does not identify the source
A bare URL when the style requires author and date
A note that says source unknown
scenarioWhy: A citation identifies the source of the finding in the required style.

definition: The complete list of works cited in the thesis, formatted in the required style and placed at the end.
wrongs: A list of interesting books that were never cited.
The in-text author-year pointers with no full details anywhere.
The bibliography of a different thesis copied in full.
why: The reference list gives full details for every work actually cited, in the required format.
example: Every author-year citation in the chapters has a matching formatted entry in the final reference list.
scenario: An examiner finds an in-text citation with no matching full entry at the end. Which part is incomplete?
scenarioWrongs: A list of books you never cited
scenarioWhy: The reference list must contain every cited work, with full details in the required style.

definition: A brief pointer in the body of the thesis, such as an author and year, that links a claim to the reference list.
wrongs: The full reference entry placed only at the end of the thesis.
A page number with no link to any source.
A comment left in a draft and then deleted.
why: An in-text citation is the short marker beside the claim that points to a full reference.
example: The sentence ends with (Adeyemi, 2022), and that name and year appear in the reference list.
scenario: A claim needs a short pointer in the paragraph, not the full reference typed out each time. Which device is that?
scenarioWrongs: Only the full entry at the end of the thesis
scenarioWhy: An in-text citation is the brief pointer in the paragraph that links a claim to the reference list.

definition: A restatement of a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure, still accompanied by a citation.
wrongs: A copy of the source's sentences with a few synonyms swapped and no citation.
The source's exact words inside quotation marks and cited.
Your own finding that did not come from a source.
why: Paraphrase uses your own wording and structure and still credits the source of the idea.
example: The student rewrites a paper's conclusion about video length in new sentences and cites the paper.
scenario: You want to use a paper's idea without copying its sentences. Which approach is an acceptable paraphrase?
scenarioAnswer: Rewrite the idea in your own structure and cite it
scenarioWrongs: Swap a few synonyms and omit the citation
Keep the exact sentences even with a citation, and call that a paraphrase
Present the idea as if you had discovered it
scenarioWhy: A paraphrase restates the idea in your own words and structure and still cites the source.

definition: The exact words of a source, clearly marked as a quote and cited, used when the original wording itself matters.
wrongs: Exact words woven into your paragraph with no marks and no citation.
A paraphrase that does not keep the original wording.
A sentence you wrote yourself.
why: A quotation reproduces exact wording, marks it as such, and cites the source.
example: A distinctive definition is placed in quotation marks with the author, year, and page, because the wording is the point.
scenario: The source's exact definition must appear because its wording matters. Which presentation is a proper quotation?
scenarioAnswer: The exact words in quotation marks with a citation
scenarioWrongs: The exact words with no marks and no citation
A rewrite in your own words
scenarioWhy: A quotation is exact wording, marked and cited, used when the original words matter.

definition: Presenting another person's words, ideas, figures, or code as your own, whether or not the copying was intentional.
wrongs: A marked quotation with a full citation.
A paraphrase in your own structure that cites the source.
Data you collected and reported yourself.
why: Plagiarism is uncredited use of someone else's work, and it does not require an intention to cheat.
example: A discussion paragraph copies a blog's sentences and does not cite the blog, so the marker records plagiarism.
scenario: A paragraph copies a blog and gives no source, though you say you forgot. Which judgement still fits?
scenarioWrongs: It is a proper quotation because you meant well
scenarioWhy: Presenting someone else's words as your own without credit is plagiarism even when it was not deliberate.

definition: Reusing your own earlier assessed work as if it were new, without disclosure and the permission your department requires.
wrongs: Citing your earlier essay and using only a short quoted extract with permission.
Writing a new chapter that refers to your previous study and cites it.
Submitting work that has never been assessed before.
why: Self-plagiarism is undisclosed reuse of your own previous assessed work, which departments treat as misconduct.
example: The student pastes a whole coursework essay into the literature chapter and does not say it was previously graded.
scenario: You paste a previously graded essay into the thesis and do not disclose it. Which problem is that?
scenarioWrongs: A short cited extract used with permission
A new chapter that cites your earlier study
Work that has never been assessed
scenarioWhy: Undisclosed reuse of your own assessed work is self-plagiarism.

definition: Honesty in study and research, including proper credit, truthful data, and submission of work you are entitled to claim.
wrongs: A high mark obtained by hiding sources or inventing data.
Letting someone else write the thesis and submitting it as yours.
A rule that applies only during exams and not to the thesis.
why: Academic integrity requires honest credit, truthful evidence, and work that is genuinely the student's to submit.
example: The student cites every borrowed figure, reports a non-significant result, and confirms the writing is their own.
scenario: You could hide a source or invent a result to look stronger. Which choice shows academic integrity?
scenarioAnswer: Cite the source and report the real result
scenarioWrongs: Hide the source to raise the mark
Invent data that fit the aim
Submit a thesis someone else wrote
scenarioWhy: Academic integrity means honest credit, truthful data, and work you are entitled to claim.

definition: The chapter that explains and justifies how evidence was collected and analysed so a reader can judge the study.
wrongs: A chapter that only lists findings with no account of how they were produced.
A diary of personal feelings about the supervisor.
The title page.
why: The methodology chapter justifies the research design and the procedures for collection and analysis.
example: The chapter explains the two groups, the call-count measure, the sample, and why a comparison of means was used.
scenario: Examiners ask how the call data were collected and why that analysis was chosen. Which chapter should answer?
scenarioWrongs: A results chapter that hides the method
scenarioWhy: The methodology chapter explains and justifies collection and analysis.

definition: The overall plan that links the question to the kind of evidence collected and how that evidence will be interpreted.
wrongs: The visual layout of the printed thesis.
The brand of laptop used for writing.
A single survey question taken out of the whole plan.
why: Research design is the plan connecting the question to evidence and interpretation.
example: The design is a two-group comparison in one university, using call counts as the outcome.
scenario: You must show how the question leads to two groups and a call-count comparison. Which plan is that?
scenarioWrongs: One survey question with no overall plan
scenarioWhy: Research design is the overall link from the question to the evidence and how it will be interpreted.

definition: The procedures used to gather the evidence the thesis later analyses.
wrongs: The statistical test run after the evidence is already in hand.
The literature search for other people's studies.
Proofreading the finished chapters.
why: Data collection is how the study's own evidence is gathered, before it is analysed.
example: Help-desk logs are exported for the month after the video, using a procedure described in the thesis.
scenario: You export help-desk logs for the study month using a stated procedure. Which activity is that?
scenarioWhy: Gathering the study's evidence by a stated procedure is data collection.

definition: The procedures used to turn the collected evidence into findings, such as a statistical test or thematic coding.
wrongs: The act of gathering the logs or interviews.
Choosing the font for the results tables.
Writing the acknowledgements.
why: Data analysis transforms collected evidence into findings; it is not the collection step itself.
example: The student compares the two groups' call counts with the test named in the methodology.
scenario: The logs are already gathered, and you now compare the two groups with the planned test. Which step is that?
scenarioWhy: Turning collected evidence into findings with a stated procedure is data analysis.

definition: The chapter that reports what the analysis found, without yet making the full interpretive argument.
wrongs: The chapter that mainly compares the findings with other authors and states implications.
The methods chapter.
The reference list.
why: The results chapter presents findings; extended interpretation belongs in the discussion.
example: The chapter reports the group means, the test result, and a table, and does not yet argue what managers should do.
scenario: You need to report means and the test result before arguing what they imply. Which chapter should hold those findings?
scenarioWrongs: A chapter devoted to implications and other authors
scenarioWhy: The results chapter reports what was found, leaving the fuller interpretation to the discussion.

definition: A numbered display of evidence, with a caption, that presents data or a diagram the text then explains.
wrongs: An unnumbered image pasted with no caption and never mentioned.
A decorative border on the title page.
A table of contents.
why: Tables and figures are numbered, captioned displays of evidence that the prose must explain.
example: Table 2 shows mean calls by group, is numbered and captioned, and is discussed in the following paragraph.
scenario: Mean calls by group need a numbered, captioned display that the text explains. Which element is that?
scenarioWrongs: An unnumbered image never mentioned in the text
scenarioWhy: A table is a numbered, captioned display of evidence that the surrounding text explains.

definition: The chapter that interprets the results, compares them with the literature, and states what they mean for the question.
wrongs: A chapter that only reprints the results tables and adds no interpretation.
The methodology chapter.
The acknowledgements.
why: The discussion interprets findings against the question and the literature; it does not merely repeat tables.
example: The chapter argues that the drop in calls fits two earlier studies and does not support a claim about other universities.
scenario: The means are already reported. You now need to say what they mean and how they compare with earlier studies. Which chapter is that?
scenarioWrongs: A second copy of the results tables with no comment
scenarioWhy: The discussion interprets results, compares them with the literature, and answers the question.

definition: A weakness in scope, method, or data that bounds how far the findings should be taken, and that is stated openly.
wrongs: A secret flaw the student hopes examiners will not notice.
Proof that the study is worthless and should be thrown away.
A spelling mistake in the title.
why: A limitation is an honest bound on the findings, not a reason to hide weakness or to abandon every claim.
example: The thesis states that one college and a convenience sample limit generalisation to other universities.
scenario: The sample came from one college and was convenient to reach. Where should that bound on the findings be stated?
scenarioWrongs: Nowhere, in the hope it stays unnoticed
As proof the whole thesis must be discarded
scenarioWhy: A limitation openly bounds how far findings can be taken, such as weak generalisation from one college.

definition: The closing chapter that answers the aim, summarises the contribution, and does not introduce new evidence.
wrongs: A chapter that presents new tables never shown in the results.
The literature review.
A chapter that avoids answering the aim.
why: The conclusion answers the aim from evidence already presented and does not add new findings.
example: The final chapter states that the video met the aim of reducing calls in this setting and points to the stated limits.
scenario: You are closing the thesis and are tempted to add a new table. Which rule applies to the conclusion chapter?
scenarioAnswer: Answer the aim without introducing new evidence
scenarioWrongs: Add new tables that were never in the results
Avoid saying whether the aim was met
scenarioWhy: The conclusion answers the aim and summarises the contribution without new evidence.

definition: A practical suggestion, grounded in the findings, about what a practitioner or researcher should do next.
wrongs: Advice that ignores the findings and repeats a personal preference.
A new result hidden inside the suggestion.
A requirement that the university must obey the student.
why: A recommendation is practical advice justified by the findings already reported.
example: Because calls fell in this setting, the thesis recommends a pilot of the short video on one further faculty before a full rollout.
scenario: The findings show fewer calls in this setting only. Which recommendation is grounded in that finding?
scenarioAnswer: Pilot the video on one further faculty before a full rollout
scenarioWrongs: Roll it out worldwide because you prefer videos
Hide a new unreported dataset inside the advice
Require the university to obey you
scenarioWhy: A recommendation is a practical next step justified by the findings, matched to their limits.

definition: Specific studies or improvements the thesis identifies as worthwhile but does not itself complete.
wrongs: Work the thesis has already finished and reported.
A vague statement that more research is needed, with no specific study.
The supervisor's unrelated grant, never mentioned in the findings.
why: Future work names concrete follow-on studies that the present thesis leaves open.
example: The thesis proposes a later random sample across three universities, which this study did not attempt.
scenario: Your sample was one college, and you want to name a study you did not do. Which statement is future work?
scenarioAnswer: A later random sample across three universities
scenarioWrongs: Repeating the analysis you already reported
Saying only that more research is needed
scenarioWhy: Future work specifies a worthwhile study the thesis itself does not complete.

definition: A formal examination in which the student presents the thesis and answers questions from the examiners.
wrongs: A private chat with friends about the topic.
Submitting the PDF with no questioning.
The literature-search stage at the start of the year.
why: The oral defence is the live examination of the student's understanding of their submitted thesis.
example: The student gives a short presentation and then answers examiners' questions about the sample and the statistics.
scenario: After submission, examiners will question you in person about the thesis. Which event is that?
scenarioWhy: The oral defence is the formal session where you present the thesis and answer examiners.

definition: The examiners appointed to read the thesis and question the student in the oral defence.
wrongs: The student's family sitting in the audience.
The classmates who proofread a draft.
The IT help desk.
why: The defence committee is the appointed examining panel, not the audience or informal helpers.
example: Two examiners who read the thesis form the committee and lead the questioning.
scenario: You must know who is appointed to read the thesis and question you. Which group is that?
scenarioWhy: The defence committee is the panel of examiners appointed to read and question.

definition: A question in the defence that probes the method, findings, limitations, or the student's own contribution.
wrongs: A request to read the abstract aloud with no follow-up.
A question about an unrelated module's exam.
A question the student wrote for a survey participant.
why: A viva question tests the student's command of the thesis, including method and limits.
example: An examiner asks why a convenience sample was acceptable and what it prevents the thesis from claiming.
scenario: An examiner asks why your sample limits generalisation. Which kind of question is that?
scenarioWrongs: A request only to read the abstract aloud
A question from an unrelated exam
A survey item you wrote for participants
scenarioWhy: A viva question probes the thesis itself, such as a limitation of the method.

definition: Comments from the supervisor on drafts, which the student should address or explicitly justify not following.
wrongs: Comments the student may ignore with no reason.
The examiners' questions at the defence, which come later.
Automated spelling highlights only, with no supervisor involved.
why: Supervisor feedback is guidance on drafts that the student must answer, either by changes or by a stated reason.
example: The supervisor says the gap is unclear, and the student rewrites the end of the literature chapter.
scenario: Your supervisor writes that the literature gap is unclear. Which response handles that feedback properly?
scenarioAnswer: Revise the gap or explain why you did not
scenarioWrongs: Ignore the comment with no reason
Wait for the defence and hope it disappears
Treat a spellchecker underline as the supervisor's comment
scenarioWhy: Supervisor feedback on a draft should be addressed or explicitly justified.

definition: A schedule of milestones, such as proposal, ethics, draft chapters, and submission, used to keep the project on track.
wrongs: A wish to finish someday with no dates.
The university's bus timetable.
The reference list sorted by year.
why: A thesis timeline sets dated milestones so proposal, ethics, drafting, and submission stay feasible.
example: The plan dates the proposal in week 3, ethics in week 5, the methodology draft in week 8, and submission in week 14.
scenario: Ethics, the methodology draft, and submission have no dates and are starting to collide. Which artefact should set those dates?
scenarioWrongs: A note that says finish someday
scenarioWhy: A thesis timeline schedules milestones such as ethics, drafts, and submission.

definition: Formal permission, granted before data collection, that the study's treatment of people or data meets institutional rules.
wrongs: Permission sought after the interviews have already been completed.
A friend's verbal encouragement to start.
Approval of the writing style by the supervisor, with no ethics review.
why: Ethics approval is institutional permission that must be in place before data are collected from people.
example: The student waits for the committee's approval letter before sending the survey to classmates.
scenario: You want to survey classmates next week, and the committee has not replied. Which condition must you have first?
scenarioWrongs: A plan to ask for approval after the survey
Approval of your paragraph style only
scenarioWhy: Ethics approval is formal permission required before collection from participants.

definition: An automated comparison of the thesis text with other sources, used as a prompt to check citation rather than as a final verdict.
wrongs: A guarantee that a low score means there is no plagiarism.
A guarantee that a high score means misconduct, even when quotations are cited.
The examiner's mark for the oral defence.
why: A similarity report flags overlapping text for human checking; the score alone is not a judgement of misconduct.
example: A high score comes from properly quoted method text, so the student checks the citations rather than assuming guilt.
scenario: The report score is high because of long cited quotations. Which interpretation is sound?
scenarioAnswer: Check the matches and citations; the score is not itself a verdict
scenarioWrongs: A low score would have proved there was no plagiarism
A high score automatically means misconduct
The score is the defence mark
scenarioWhy: A similarity report prompts checking of overlap and citation; it does not by itself decide misconduct.

definition: The required rules for how in-text citations and the reference list are formatted, such as APA or IEEE.
wrongs: A personal mix of several styles in one thesis.
The writing font required by the department.
A rule about the colour of the cover.
why: A citation style is a consistent set of rules for citations and references, chosen as the department requires.
example: The department requires IEEE, so numbered citations and the matching reference format are used throughout.
scenario: The department requires one referencing format, and your draft mixes two. Which requirement are you breaking?
scenarioWhy: Citation style is the single required format for in-text citations and the reference list.

definition: A persistent identifier for a digital publication, used in a reference so readers can locate that exact work.
wrongs: The student's university ID number.
A temporary search URL that may stop working.
The page count of the thesis.
why: A DOI is a stable identifier for a published work and is preferred in references when the style asks for it.
example: The reference for a journal article ends with the DOI rather than a long search-page link.
scenario: The style asks for a stable identifier for a journal article, not a search-page link that may die. Which identifier fits?
scenarioWhy: A DOI persistently identifies the exact digital publication for the reference.

definition: A work written for an academic audience and typically reviewed or issued by a recognised scholarly publisher.
wrongs: An anonymous promotional post by a vendor.
A friend's unreferenced opinion in a chat.
A headline with no named author or evidence.
why: A scholarly source is aimed at an academic audience and usually passes some form of editorial or peer review.
example: The student cites a reviewed journal article on training videos instead of a vendor's promotional post.
scenario: You need a source an examiner will treat as academic evidence about training videos. Which source fits?
scenarioWhy: A reviewed article for an academic audience is a scholarly source.

definition: A literature review organised by themes or debates, rather than by a sequence of separate paper summaries.
wrongs: A review that gives one paragraph to each paper in date order only.
A chronological diary of the student's reading week.
The results chapter.
why: A thematic review groups sources under themes so agreements and disagreements become visible.
example: One section covers video length, another covers call-volume measures, and papers are discussed inside those themes.
scenario: Your draft is one paragraph per paper in date order. Which reorganisation makes it a thematic review?
scenarioAnswer: Group the papers under themes such as video length and outcome measures
scenarioWrongs: Keep one paragraph per paper in date order
Replace it with a diary of your reading week
Move the results tables into the review
scenarioWhy: A thematic review organises the literature by themes or debates rather than paper by paper.

definition: A short passage that states what the literature does not yet answer and that this thesis will address.
wrongs: A sentence that says the literature is complete and no study is needed.
The abstract's summary of findings.
A list of every paper ever published on the topic.
why: The gap statement identifies the unanswered point that justifies the thesis.
example: The review ends by stating that no study has measured reset calls after a short video for first-year students.
scenario: The review never says what is still unknown. Which sentence should you add at its end?
scenarioAnswer: A gap statement naming the unanswered call-rate question
scenarioWrongs: A claim that the literature is already complete
An unfiltered list of every paper
scenarioWhy: A gap statement says what the literature has not answered and what the thesis will address.

definition: The specific addition the thesis makes to knowledge or practice, stated so examiners can see what is new.
wrongs: A restatement of the aim with no indication of what was added.
A claim to have solved every related problem in the field.
The supervisor's earlier publication presented as the student's own.
why: The contribution is the particular new result, design, or understanding this thesis provides.
example: The thesis contributes evidence that a two-minute video was followed by fewer reset calls in one college.
scenario: Examiners ask what your thesis adds that the cited papers did not already show. Which answer states a contribution?
scenarioAnswer: Evidence on reset calls after a short video in this college
scenarioWrongs: A repeat of the aim with nothing new identified
A claim to have solved the whole field
Your supervisor's paper presented as yours
scenarioWhy: The contribution is the specific addition this thesis makes, matched to its evidence.

definition: The boundary of what the study includes and excludes, set so the project is completable and the claims match the evidence.
wrongs: A promise to study every university and every security topic.
The page margins required by the template.
The list of people thanked.
why: Scope draws a boundary around a completable study and keeps claims inside that boundary.
example: The thesis includes first-year students at one college and excludes staff accounts and other institutions.
scenario: You are tempted to claim the video works for every university, but you studied one college. Which boundary should you state?
scenarioAnswer: The scope covering that college and excluding others
scenarioWrongs: A scope of every university and every topic
scenarioWhy: The scope of the thesis is the boundary of inclusion and exclusion that claims must respect.

definition: Supplementary material, such as a questionnaire or extra tables, placed after the references and referred to from the main text.
wrongs: A place to hide results that are essential and never mentioned in the chapters.
The abstract.
A second copy of the whole thesis.
why: An appendix holds supplementary material that the main text points to, not core results with no mention.
example: The survey form is placed in Appendix A, and the methodology chapter tells the reader to consult it.
scenario: The survey form is too long for the methodology chapter but examiners may need it. Where should it go?
scenarioAnswer: In an appendix referred to from the chapter
scenarioWrongs: Nowhere, while the results depend on a form nobody can see
As a duplicate of the entire thesis
scenarioWhy: An appendix holds supplementary material, such as a questionnaire, that the main text cites.

definition: An alphabetical list of specialist terms and their meanings, included when readers may not share the thesis vocabulary.
wrongs: The reference list of cited works.
A list of figures.
The index of authors, if the terms themselves are not defined.
why: A glossary defines specialist terms for the reader and is distinct from the references.
example: The glossary defines reset call and convenience sample in a few plain sentences each.
scenario: Examiners outside your lab may not know your specialist terms. Which list should define them?
scenarioWrongs: An author index with no definitions
scenarioWhy: A glossary is an alphabetical list of specialist terms and their meanings.

definition: A short section thanking people and organisations that helped, which does not add academic claims.
wrongs: The chapter that answers the research aim.
A place to put new results.
The reference list.
why: Acknowledgements thank helpers and are not part of the academic argument or the evidence.
example: The student thanks the supervisor and the help-desk team for access to anonymised call counts.
scenario: You want to thank the supervisor and the help-desk team without adding findings. Which section is appropriate?
scenarioWrongs: The conclusion, as if thanks were a finding
scenarioWhy: The acknowledgement thanks contributors and does not carry academic claims.

definition: The front page that states the thesis title, author, award, institution, and submission date in the required format.
wrongs: The abstract.
A decorative cover with only an image and no identifying text.
The first page of the literature review.
why: The title page identifies the work, the author, and the award in the format the institution specifies.
example: The first page shows the title, the student's name, the degree, the university, and the submission month.
scenario: The template requires the title, your name, the degree, the university, and the date on the front. Which page is that?
scenarioWhy: The title page carries the identifying details of the thesis in the required format.

definition: A final check of spelling, grammar, citations, numbering, and cross-references before the thesis is submitted.
wrongs: Adding a new experiment the week of submission.
Choosing the research question.
Collecting the original data.
why: Proofreading is the last check of presentation and consistency, not a stage for new research.
example: The student checks that Table 2 is cited, that every citation is in the reference list, and that chapter numbers match the contents.
scenario: Submission is tomorrow and the analysis is finished. Which final task is proofreading?
scenarioAnswer: Check spelling, citation matches, and numbering
scenarioWhy: Proofreading is the final check of language, citations, numbering, and cross-references.

definition: A written reply, after review or the defence, that states how each required change was made or why a comment was not followed.
wrongs: A reply that ignores required changes and resubmits the same file.
The original proposal from the start of the year.
A thank-you card with no account of the changes.
why: A response to examiners accounts for each required change so the revised thesis can be checked.
example: The student lists each examiner comment, notes the page of the revision, and explains one suggestion they did not adopt.
scenario: Examiners require changes and a resubmission. Which document should explain how each comment was handled?
scenarioWrongs: The same file with the comments ignored
A thank-you card with no change log
scenarioWhy: A response to examiners states how each required change was made or justified.

definition: A signed statement that the thesis is the student's own work, except where sources and help are properly acknowledged.
wrongs: A promise that no source was consulted at all.
The supervisor's signature in place of the student's.
A claim that a purchased essay is acceptable if it matches the title.
why: A declaration of originality confirms the student is entitled to submit the work and has acknowledged help and sources.
example: The student signs the department form stating the thesis is their own, aside from cited material and declared assistance.
scenario: The template asks you to confirm the thesis is your own work except for acknowledged help. Which statement is that?
scenarioWrongs: A promise that you read nothing
The supervisor's signature instead of yours
A receipt for a purchased essay
scenarioWhy: The declaration of originality is the student's signed statement that the thesis is their own acknowledged work.
